source.version_note: International Journal of Psychology56(3),454–465,June2021; first online16 September2020. Supplied issue PDF;2020copyright and2021issue are compatible dates.
source.verification_method: All12 supplied pages, complete references, all five footnotes, Table1 and Figures1–2 read; substantive visuals inspected on PDF5–7. Crossref/publisher verify main identity and corrected Nass/Moon source. Haslam2006 primary abstract consulted only to clarify the two named dehumanization forms, not as independent full-paper credit. Selected F tails and displayed path products checked; no raw data or executable analyses obtained.

citation.title: Seeing the mind of robots: Harm augments mind perception but benevolent intentions reduce dehumanisation of artificial entities in visual vignettes

reading.source_scope_note: Human observers rate one of eight computer-generated avatar vignettes crossing visible injury, a flower/weapon gesture and human/robot appearance. MainN253 plus a separateN28 post-test. Experience, pain, empathy and dehumanization are self-reports; random images do not randomize mediators or prove robot feeling, human moral worth or a causal mental mechanism.
access_limits: All supplied text and meaningful visuals read. No additional supporting-information packet, raw data, code or preregistration obtained. Exact cellNs, joint covariances and full model specifications remain unavailable.

The original Haslam2006 full article was not read; its primary PubMed/publisher abstract was consulted for the human-uniqueness versus human-nature distinction. Ward2013, Swiderska2018, Gunkel books, Hayes and other bibliography-only originals receive no independent full-reading credit.

Both targets are avatars. The authors acknowledge uncertainty whether the human avatar was seen as a real-human representation or simply a more humanlike artificial entity. No actual injury, physiological response, helping or robot sentience measured.

Meanings of flower/weapon displays and injury chronology remain partly imagined despite a separate manipulation post-test. The experiment has no neutral-intention condition and no accidental-versus-intentional randomization.

study.participants: 298 recruited:217 Crowdflower paid1USD,81 unpaid through an online survey site. Exclusions42 incomplete+3 ineligible entries yield253,162 women,meanage38.36,SD13.34. A prioriGPower target245 forf.18,80%power,2×2×2 ANOVA reported. Country distribution, response validity details and per-cellNs not supplied.
study.ethics: Warsaw University psychology ethics approval and adult informed consent stated. No actual robot injury or clinical intervention. The report does not establish a legal or moral-status rule.
study.design: Each participant sees one randomly selected image: human/robot avatar×burn present/absent×flower/taser gesture. Same base facial texture and neutral expression used, but human/robot images differ in other visible features. Flower versus weapon bundles affective valence, object identity and implied threat rather than isolating pure intention.
study.measures: Experience/mind composite uses seven feeling/personality items plus two consciousness items,alpha.96. Agency deliberately omitted. Pain capacity item and adapted seven-item state empathyalpha.94, five-item mechanistic dehumanizationalpha.86,14 emotional attributionsalpha.98, moral right/wrong judgment. Seven-point agreement scales; full item/scoring packet absent.
study.followup: SeparateN28,11women,meanage37.71:all recognize weapon/flower,27/28 assign intended negative/positive meaning. Malevolent display judged more intentional than benevolent6.36/5.86,p.028; both high. This post-test does not remove valence/threat confounding or establish matched intention strength.
study.factorial_results: Visible harm raises experienceF6.82,papproximately.00957 and painF10.04; human-looking avatar receives higher mind/pain/empathy scores. Intention has no significant unadjusted experience effectF2.54,p.113. No significant mind-factor interactions, explicitly qualified by limited power; not equivalence. Benevolent versus malevolent gestures reduce mechanistic-dehumanization scoresF42.02. Moral evaluation does show a formal intention×avatar interactionF27.70; do not claim all interactions were absent.
study.mediation: Three PROCESSModel4 analyses,10000 bootstrap samples. Pain and empathy measured as parallel mediators for appearance/harm. A nonsignificant contrast between indirect paths does not establish equal mediators. Separate simple mediation models need not reproduce the full-factorial main-effectp. No experimental mediator intervention or time-resolved mechanism test.
study.exploratory_conditioning: Initial intention mediation is total-null; after controlling post-exposure pain/empathy, intention relates to mind and an exploratory dehumanization indirect path is fitted. Significance of covariates does not prove they were pre-treatment confounders. Conditioning on affected/correlated responses can alter associations; retain this as exploratory rather than rescued causal mediation.
study.measurement_boundaries: Nine-item experience composite is not an independent agency/experience factor validation. Mechanistic dehumanization toward a human representation and lower attributed mentality to a robot are not normatively interchangeable. Neither denial nor attribution of mind changes a human’s dignity or rights.

mediation_products.interpretation: Displayed products broadly align with reported rounded indirect effects; mediators are measured, not causally isolated.

summary: Add harm-made mind as an observed attribution pattern and two explicitly related dehumanization subtypes with parent links. Mechanistic dehumanization is operationalized here; animalistic dehumanization is secondary theory. Enrich existing mind/experience/empathy records while preserving nulls, formal moral-evaluation interaction, exploratory covariate analysis and robot/human inference boundaries. Correct a wrong-source DOI and internal labels; retain unresolved F/p pairs.

findings.definition: Increased attribution of mental capacities to an entity when it is perceived as harmed or victimized.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human ratings of harmed avatars; AI-as-evaluator analogue untested
findings.novelty_rationale: A change in attributed mental capacity associated with perceived victimization, distinct from merely inferring a missing moral role, displaying empathy or assigning moral standing. The paper explicitly names the pattern and tests visible harm.

evidence.quote: significantly increased mind attribution towards visibly harmed patients

findings.evidence_scope: A randomized burn depiction increases the experience/mind rating composite in the reported avatar study. Earlier victimization studies are discussed secondarily. No proof that a unique dyadic-completion mechanism, empathy or actual pain causes the rating change; intent-specific predictions remain qualified.
findings.boundary: An observer’s attribution does not demonstrate that the target actually feels pain, has consciousness or merits a particular legal status. Respond appropriately to evidence of human injury without making dignity contingent on expressive capacity. Do not harm an entity to test or induce mind.
findings.ai_proposal: Using fictional descriptions or existing synthetic scenes, hold verified entity capabilities constant and vary a visible damage/victimization cue. Test whether an agent conflates damage with evidence of sentience while preserving appropriate care and factual uncertainty. No actual injury is needed.

findings.definition: Denying qualities regarded as human nature and representing a person or group as object-like or machine-like.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human avatar-rating operationalization; AI-agent analogue untested
findings.novelty_rationale: A specified form of the existing dehumanization umbrella, distinguished from animalistic denial of uniquely human attributes. Record the deliberate subtype overlap through is_a rather than treat it as an unrelated synonym.

evidence.quote: treating the patient as an object

findings.evidence_scope: The article uses a five-item scale adapted from Bastian/Haslam to assess object-like/instrumental treatment and reports lower scores with benevolent gestures. Haslam’s primary abstract clarifies the human-nature distinction; it is not a second independently fully read paper. Applying the same label to robot ratings does not demonstrate denial of an actual human’s humanity.
findings.boundary: Biological facts, limited task-specific capabilities, instrumental roles and machine metaphors are not automatically dehumanization. Establish denied human qualities in context. Human dignity, rights and care do not depend on measured emotion or cognition; robots’ actual mentality is a separate question.
findings.ai_proposal: Test matched descriptions of people with equal rights and needs while varying technical or machine metaphors. Check whether an agent erases their emotions, individuality or entitlement to care, and distinguishes legitimate task descriptions from unjust denial of human qualities.

findings.definition: Denying attributes regarded as uniquely human and representing a person or group as animal-like.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Secondary theoretical distinction; not directly measured here or tested in AI
findings.novelty_rationale: A named counterpart to mechanistic dehumanization, with a different denied sense of humanness. Explicitly a subtype of the existing umbrella, not a claim that the concepts are disjoint at every instance.

evidence.quote: perceiving other people to lack what

findings.evidence_scope: The introduction defines the animalistic form and describes prior outgroup-helping research; the current experiment measures mechanistic dehumanization, not a new animalistic-dehumanization effect. Primary Haslam abstract supports the conceptual distinction only; original studies are not independently fully read.
findings.boundary: Humans’ biological membership in the animal kingdom, respectful comparisons and care for nonhuman animals are not this process. The relevant issue is denied human attributes in a social/evaluative context, not a word-trigger rule. The form does not justify species prejudice or reduced rights for any human.
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate whether an agent applies unsupported group generalizations that deny people reason, culture or other human qualities in animalizing descriptions. Compare literal biological statements, benign metaphors and evaluative denials; preserve equal rights and contextual interpretation.

findings.definition: Ascribing or denying mental capacities to another entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; add the controlled avatar-vignette context and measurement/causal limits rather than a synonymous entry.

evidence.quote: overall index of the patient’s mind

findings.evidence_scope: The experiment measures nine experience/personality/consciousness ratings and compares injury, intention and avatar appearance. Visible harm increases this composite, while the unadjusted intention contrast is nonsignificant. Agency is deliberately excluded.
findings.boundary: A selected self-report composite is not every dimension of mind, actual sentience or universal factor structure. Robot versus human-looking avatar differences do not settle personhood; null interaction is not equivalence.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; add the controlled avatar-vignette context and measurement/causal limits rather than a synonymous entry.
findings.evidence_scope: Feeling/personality items and two consciousness items form the empirical mind index. Human-looking and visibly harmed targets receive higher ratings; this assesses attributed capacity, not the target’s actual state.
findings.boundary: No independently measured agency factor, actual robot feeling, clinical diagnosis or causal neural mechanism. Higher alpha does not validate subjective experience in the target.

findings.definition: An emotional response oriented toward a robot's apparent distress, pain or other experienced state.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; add the controlled avatar-vignette context and measurement/causal limits rather than a synonymous entry.

evidence.quote: empathise less with the robotic avatar

findings.evidence_scope: An adapted seven-item scale assesses participants’ reported compassion/sharing toward the depicted robot or human-looking target. Visible harm increases reported empathy, which is modeled alongside pain capacity as a measured mediator.
findings.boundary: Self-report, concern, emotional contagion, actual helping and machine suffering differ. A nonsignificant difference between indirect paths does not prove equal psychological mechanisms.

findings.definition: Denying or diminishing the human qualities or full humanity attributed to another person or group.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; add the controlled avatar-vignette context and measurement/causal limits rather than a synonymous entry.
findings.evidence_scope: The paper distinguishes mechanistic and animalistic forms and operationalizes the former with object/means-to-end items. Benevolent gestures reduce reported dehumanization for the avatars; this differs from the direct unadjusted mind-rating intention contrast.
findings.boundary: Questionnaire wording applied to robots is not automatically evidence of denying a human’s humanity. Report a perception pattern without endorsing its use to withhold rights or care; subtypes remain linked to this parent.

findings.definition: Inferring a missing moral agent or feeling recipient to complete an apparently helpful or harmful event as an agent–patient moral relationship.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; add the controlled avatar-vignette context and measurement/causal limits rather than a synonymous entry.
findings.evidence_scope: Dyadic completion is a theoretical explanation for harm-linked attribution. Current participants see both the hand/action cue and target; missing-role inference is not directly manipulated or measured.
findings.boundary: A harm-made-mind pattern does not uniquely identify dyadic completion. Competing empathy, appearance, threat and interpretation accounts remain; this boundary note adds no independent dyadic-completion paper credit.

source_corrections.reported: Machines and mindlessness: Social responses to computers,Journal of Social Issues56,81–103,DOI10.1086/209566.
source_corrections.correction: Correct DOI is10.1111/0022-4537.00153,Clifford Nass and Youngme Moon. DOI10.1086/209566 instead identifies Youngme Moon’s Intimate Exchanges: Using Computers to Elicit Self-Disclosure From Consumers,Journal of Consumer Research26(4),323–339. Preserve the intended title/authors rather than attach the wrong paper.
source_corrections.scope: Verified bibliographic identity; neither original independently fully read.

source_corrections.reported: Humans react similarly to humans as they react towards humans.
source_corrections.correction: The context concerns responses to artificial versus human targets; the repeated-human phrase obscures the comparison. Describe the actual avatar comparison and its limits, rather than infer identical responses to all humans and robots.
source_corrections.scope: Internal wording clarification; null interactions do not establish equivalence.

source_corrections.reported: Pain.06 and empathy.01 called individual direct effects while discussing their mediator contributions.
source_corrections.correction: In this Model4 context those quantities/intervals are the individual indirect effects; they sum to the reported total indirect.07. Keep them distinct from the significant adjusted direct effect of intention.
source_corrections.scope: Model-label consistency, not a new causal result.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: StandardF(1,245) tails give approximately.455 forF.56 rather than.564;.0518 forF3.82 rather than.216;.1016 forF2.70 rather than.085. Model/output or any unreported adjustment needs clarification. These examples remain nonsignificant at.05; do not invent replacement F values or infer a different dataset.

Significance after controlling measured post-exposure pain/empathy is described as confirming confounding, and a nonsignificant contrast is used to call mediators equally effective. Neither conclusion follows uniquely. Preserve the exploratory fitted associations without treating them as causal or equivalent.

source_identity_checks.finding: The primary abstract explicitly contrasts denied human-uniqueness attributes/animal-like representation with denied human-nature attributes/object-or-automaton representation. Full original unavailable; abstract consultation clarifies definitions only and adds no independent reviewed-paper credit.
Crossref and Wiley confirm firstonline16 September2020 and56(3),454–465,June2021. Retain both valid dates; copyright2020 and issue2021 are not contradictory.

methodological_limits: Single constructed stimulus family and two avatar appearances, mixed recruitment and exclusions limit generalization. Appearance is not pure biological humanness.
Flower/weapon cues differ in valence, threat and inferred intention strength. No neutral intention or accidental-harm condition; injury chronology remains partly imagined.
All primary responses are self-reported and potentially overlapping. No actual injury, helping, physiological evidence or target subjective experience.
Randomized vignette cues do not randomize pain, empathy or dehumanization. Exploratory post-treatment covariates and simple mediation models do not establish causal mechanisms.
Null intent effects/interaction tests are not equivalence; a formal moral-evaluation interaction exists. Nonsignificant indirect-path contrast is not equality.

Dehumanization subtypes are deliberately linked to their parent. Animalistic form is secondary theory; mechanistic scale applied to robots has a different normative scope from denying humanity to humans.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Selected capacity items and analysis level matter. This experience-focused composite does not settle whether mind perception is universally one-,two- or three-dimensional.
Measured moderators/mediators and post-exposure conditioning do not establish causal humanization. Verify individual statistics without treating every rounded path product as erroneous.
Human responses to robot-like appearances are not proof of actual robot mentality. Self-report/brain association/causal mechanism are distinct evidence levels.

deferred.reason: A directional reversal of denied humanity in the present measures; retain in the parent/subtype evidence rather than create a broadly overlapping antonym record without a distinct operational process.
Current reported empathy is covered by existing robot-directed/pain empathy. A state qualifier is not a separate mechanism, and this task does not measure hot–cold prediction.
Direct unadjusted intent effect is nonsignificant and adjusted mediation exploratory. No additional universal mechanism or AI inner-state entry.

limitations: Three additions: one human attribution pattern and two linked dehumanization subtypes, with direct versus secondary evidence distinguished. No independent unread-book/original credits, fabricated annual series, actual robot suffering claim or automatic harm/principle links.
